title: India's Monsoon Forecast Just Got Worse. It Could Be the Driest Season in 11 Years.
excerpt: IMD now expects rainfall at just 90 per cent of normal — down from an already cautious 92 per cent — as an emerging El Niño threatens crops, reservoirs, and food prices across the subcontinent.
body:
The India Meteorological Department has downgraded its monsoon forecast for the second time, now projecting rainfall at just 90 per cent of the long-period average for the June-September season. If that number holds, 2026 will be India's driest monsoon year since 2015 — a prospect with far-reaching consequences for an economy already under pressure from the Iran war and soaring energy costs.

The revised forecast, released on May 30, lowers the earlier April estimate of 92 per cent. The IMD defines normal rainfall as 96-104 per cent of the 50-year average of 87 centimetres. At 90 per cent, the country would formally be in "below normal" territory, with an 84 per cent probability of deficit rainfall.

## El Niño Returns

The primary driver is the re-emergence of El Niño — the periodic warming of Pacific Ocean surface temperatures that disrupts global weather patterns. M. Ravichandran, secretary in the earth sciences ministry, confirmed that an El Niño event is likely to develop soon, with its intensity expected to range between moderate and strong during the second half of the monsoon season, precisely when India's kharif crops need the most rain.

The last consecutive drought years were 2014 and 2015, when rainfall stood at 88 per cent and 86 per cent of normal respectively. Those seasons saw sharp spikes in food prices, distress among farming communities, and forced the Reserve Bank of India to factor agricultural supply disruptions into its policy calculus.

## June Will Be Critical

June rainfall, when kharif sowing begins across the country, is projected at below 92 per cent of the long-period average. A weak start to the monsoon delays planting, reduces crop coverage, and amplifies the damage if follow-on months are also dry.

Several Indian states are already reeling under severe heatwave conditions, with temperatures exceeding 45 degrees Celsius across parts of Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Odisha. These are temperatures that ordinarily recede only when the monsoon arrives — but a delayed or weakened onset could extend the heatwave well into June.

Northwest India, the country's wheat and rice belt, is expected to be the driest region, with rainfall below 92 per cent of normal. This is particularly concerning because northwest India is also where groundwater depletion is most acute — a deficit monsoon would worsen an already critical water table situation in states like Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh.

## The Economic Fallout

The monsoon delivers roughly 70 per cent of India's annual rainfall and underpins the livelihoods of nearly half the country's population. About half of India's farmland still lacks irrigation, making the kharif season almost entirely rain-dependent.

India's finance ministry has already flagged the risk. In its latest monthly economic report, it warned that a "significant rainfall deficit coupled with current geopolitical conditions could translate into food inflation, weakening rural demand and aggregate growth."

Economists at IDFC First Bank estimate that a deficient monsoon — particularly during the critical July-August months — could push inflation to an average of 5.5 per cent, well above the current 3.48 per cent. With crude oil prices already elevated due to the Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz blockade, a food price shock would compound the inflationary pressure and narrow the RBI's room for manoeuvre.

India's stock markets have already begun pricing in the risk. Consumer goods and automobile stocks fell 1.7 per cent and 2.3 per cent respectively on Monday, driven partly by the monsoon forecast. Foreign investors, who sold a record $2.22 billion of Indian shares on Friday during the MSCI rebalancing, are unlikely to be reassured by the weather outlook.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora, the monsoon is never just a weather event. It determines whether parents back home face water rationing, whether vegetable prices at the local market spike, and whether the agricultural communities many diaspora families come from will face another difficult year.

The RBI's monetary policy decision on Friday will be the first major policy response to the updated forecast. Economists widely expect the central bank to hold rates — but a deteriorating monsoon outlook could prompt a hawkish tilt in the committee's forward guidance, signalling readiness to tighten if food inflation spirals.

The last time India faced a genuinely poor monsoon — 2015 — rural wages stagnated, rural consumption fell, and the economic ripple effects lasted well into the following year. With the economy already absorbing the shock of $90-plus crude oil and unprecedented foreign capital outflows, a monsoon failure would test the resilience of India's growth story in a way it has not been tested in over a decade.

Sources: India Meteorological Department, Reuters, Livemint, IDFC First Bank
